title: Warning on scams, market’s dark threat
full_text:
The recent probe by the financial crimes watchdog, Austrac, dubbed Operation Claw, was a timely reminder for property industry players of the risk of scams.
It found mortgage fraud had accelerated as AI facilitated scams, hacks and fraud.
The investigation by Austrac’s private-public partnership, the Fintel Alliance across 10 major banks came upon suspected fraud enabled by fake pay slips, inflated incomes, misrepresented employment, and fabricated business activity, and much of it was created using AI to support home loans mostly linked to Sydney purchases.
It was also found that ineligible borrowers were trying to move money from China through illegitimate means.
With repeated involvement of certain accountants, law firms and mortgage brokers, there were “potentially hundreds of millions of dollars in suspected fraudulent loans.” “This is not a one-bank problem,” says Crispin Yuen, compliance specialist in Anti-Money Laundering at Custos Advisory. Last year Yuen told the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Law Enforcement’s inquiry into the capability of law enforcement to respond to money laundering and financial crime that “we are fighting 21st-century crime with 20th-century architecture”.
“The reality of modern financial crime is borderless, agile, and digital,” he said.
AUSTRAC chief executive Brendan Thomas has subsequently referred mortgage brokers, lawyers and accountants to the police, ATO and the corporate regulator, ASIC.
“Each bank may see only one fragment,” Thomas said. “When those fragments are brought together, the broader pattern becomes clear.” The discovery highlights a new front being exploited by criminals seeking to abuse Australia’s financial system.
For the past two decades the most prevalent scam has involved the individual settlement moneys of unsuspecting buyers and sellers. Some absentee property owners saw scammers from Nigeria sell their homes without their knowledge.
More commonly victims have been regularly tricked into transferring trust account funds by scammers posing as their lender. Sometimes it’s via fake email addresses and other times a phone call. Often alarmingly the scammers knew the exact amount of recent payments in each trust account which made them seem legitimate.
Confirmation of payee is a new safeguard service that banks have implemented, allowing users to check that the account name matches the intended recipient.
Other cautionary procedures exist, but settlement days can still be nerve wracking.
The recent Scams Awareness Week saw the release of data showing that payment redirection was the second most financially damaging scam in Australia for 2025, ranking behind investment scams.
Business email compromise (BEC) ranks as Australia’s fastest-growing scam category, that cost Australians $166m in 2025.
The biggest known BEC scam saw lawyers Mills Oakley sued after $928,687 went awry in 2019. Prominent Singaporean businessman Harry Chua was purchasing a Melbourne apartment in the Aurora Tower when the parties fell victim to a business email compromise scam. Chua sued Mills Oakley in 2020 to recover the lost funds, claiming the national law firm had been negligent in its cybersecurity and client verification procedures. Mills Oakley defended the allegation, maintaining the hack occurred at the client’s end. The matter was settled out of court, with the money reportedly never recovered from its Bank of China fraud account.
